la:noun:provincia.gloss: office, official duty, command, formal responsibility given to a magistrate
senses: office, official duty, command, formal responsibility given to a magistrate
the office of ruling over, or government of, an administrative region (province) of the Roman Republic or Empire
any territory outside Italy, acquired chiefly by conquest, brought under Roman rule and governed by a Roman magistrate
a territory outside of one's borders but under one's dominion
an administrative region of the Roman Republic or Roman Empire, a province
an administrative region of any government
the area oustide of Italy under Roman dominion
the Provincia Narbonensis, Provence (now part of France)
la:noun:provincia.html:
prōvincĭa, ae (old
gen. PROVINCIAI, ) [etym. dub.; perh. contr. for pro-noventia (cf. nuntius), the charge or government of a legate].
A province, i. e. a territory out of Italy, acquired by the Romans (chiefly by conquest), and brought under Roman government; freq., also, to be rendered provincial administration, employment, etc.: Sicilia prima omnium provincia est appellata,: defendo provinciam Siciliam,: provincia Syria,: Asia provincia,: provincia Gallia,: praeponere, praeficere aliquem provinciae,: tradere alicui provinciam,: in provinciam cum imperio proficisci,: administrare provinciam,: provinciam consulari imperio obtinere,; cf. : de provinciā decedere,to retire from the administration of a province,: provinciam Lentulus deposuit,gave up, resigned,: provincia consularis, governed by a former consul (proconsul), : praetoria,governed by a former prœtor,.—
In gen., a province, division of a kingdom or empire: Judaea, Esdr. 5, 8: Babylonis,.—
Transf., in gen., official duty, office, business, charge, province (class.): parasitorum,: hanc tibi impero provinciam,: abi in tuam provinciam,: duram capere provinciam,: sibi provinciam depoposcit, ut me in meo lectulo trucidaret,: qui eam provinciam susceperint, ut in balneas contruderentur,: Sicinio Volsci, Aquilio Hernici provincia evenit,i. e. were given into his charge, were assigned to him to be subdued,: cum ambo consules Appuliam provinciam haberent,.—In plur., : ipsi inter se provincias partiuntur,.

la:other:Provincia.gloss: Provence (a maritime geographic region and former province of southeastern France bordering Italy; since 2016 included in the administrative region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur)
senses: Provence (a maritime geographic region and former province of southeastern France bordering Italy; since 2016 included in the administrative region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur)

senses: to be cautious; to act with foresight
la:verb:provideo.html:
prō-vĭdĕo, vīdi, vīsum, 2, v. n. and a.
Neutr.
Lit., to see forwards or before one's self, to see in the distance, to discern, descry (very rare): ubi, quid petatur, procul provideri nequeat,.—
Trop.
To be provident or cautious, to act with foresight, to take care (rare but class.; syn. praecaveo): actum de te est, nisi provides. ; : nisi providisses, tibi ipsi pereundum fuisset,.—
To see to, look after, care for; to provide, make preparation or provision for any thing (freq. and class.); constr. absol., with dat., de, ut, ne: multum in posterum providerunt, quod, etc., : nihil me curassis, ego mihi providero,: rei frumentariae,: condicioni omnium civium,: ut consulas omnibus, ut provideas saluti,.—Impers. pass.: a dis vitae hominum consuli et provideri,: est autem de Brundusio providendum,; cf.: de re frumentariā,: de frumento,: ut quam rectissime agantur omnia providebo,.—So with ne, : cura et provide, ne quid ei desit,: ne qua civitas suis finibus recipiat, a me provisum est,; cf. impers.: provisum est, ne, etc.,: provisum atque praecautum est, ne quid, etc.,.—
Act.
Lit., to see or perceive in the distance (very rare): nave provisā,; .—
Trop.
In respect of time, to see or perceive beforehand, to foresee; to see before or earlier (class.): si qui, quae eventura sunt, provideant, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 407 Rib.); cf. : rem, quam mens providit,: quod ego, priusquam loqui coepisti, sensi atque providi,; cf. : medicus morbum ingravescentem ratione providet, insidias imperator, tempestates gubernator,: providere, quid futurum sit,: quod adhuc conjecturā provideri possit,: tempestas ante provisa,: ratio explorata atque provisa,: non hercle te provideram,: aliquem,.—
To see to, look after, care for, give attention to; to prepare or provide for any thing: eas cellas provident, ne habeant in solo umorem,: ut res tempusque postulat, provideas atque administres,: providentia haec potissimum providet, ut, etc.,: omnia,: ea, quae ad usum navium pertinerent,: rem frumentariam,; cf.: frumento exercitui proviso,: provisi ante commeatūs,: verbaque provisam rem non invita sequentur,: omnia quae multo ante memoi provisa repones,; cf.: providebam Dominum in conspectu meo, kept in view, i. e. in mind, .—
Providere aliquid, to prevent, obviate an evil (syn. cavere): neque omnino facere aut providere quicquam poterant, Kritz: quicquid provideri potest, provide,: quae consilio provideri poterunt, cavebuntur,; ; Sillig; 34, 7, 18, § 40; .—Hence,
prōvĭ-dens, entis, P. a., foreseeing, provident, prudent (class.): homo multum providens,.—Comp.: id est providentius,more prudent,.—Sup.: providentissimus quisque,; .—Adv.: prōvĭdenter, with foresight, providently, prudently, ; ; .—Comp.: quanto melius quanto providentius,.—Sup.: providentissime,; (69), 1; 10, 77 (81), 1.—*
prōvīsō, adv., with foresight or forethought, prudently: temere, proviso,.

la:adj:providus.html:
prōvĭdus, a, um, adj.
provideo
.
Foreseeing: mens provida rerum futurarum,: nec eum provida futuri, fefellit opinio,: fati,: veri providus augur,: nec futuri providus est nec praeteriti memor,.—
Cautious, circumspect, provident, prudent (syn.: cautus, consideratus): homines parum cauti providique,: animal hoc providum, sagax ... quem vocamus hominem,: orator prudens et providus,: dispice, ne sit parum providum, sperare ex aliis, quod tibi ipse non praestes,: auspex,: mens,; cf. Ulixes,.—
Caring or providing for, provident of: natura consultrix et provida utilitatum oportunitatumque omnium,: rerum vestrarum providus,: opera providae sollertisque naturae,:

provida cura ducis, .—Hence, adv.: prōvĭdē, carefully, prudently (very rare): provide eligere,.

la:verb:provoco.html:
prō-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.,
to call forth, call out.
Lit.
In gen. (very rare): aliquem,: ut ubi illaec prodeat, me provoces,; : mandant, ut ad se provocet Simonidem,: dum rota Luciferi provocet orta diem,lead up, call forth,: Memnonis mater roseo provocet ore diem,; cf. : provocare et elicere novas radiculas,.—
In partic.
To call out, challenge, invite one to any thing (as to play, sing, drink, fight, etc.): provocat me in aleam,challenged me to a game,: pedibus,to a race,: aliquem tesseris,: aliquem cantatum,: aliquem ad pugnam,; cf. , and Duker: duces nec prohibere paucos temere provocantis volebant, nec, etc., : et oleo et mero viros provocant,: aliquem ad bibendum,.—
In jurid. lang., to take a cause before a higher court, to appeal, make an appeal; in this signif. usually neutr., ad aliquem; act. only post-class., with the judge to whom the appeal is made as object (cf. appello).
Neutr.: ut de majestate damnati ad populum provocent,; cf.: quam id rectum sit, tu judicabis; ne ad Catonem quidem provocabo,: provoco ad populum,: arreptus a viatore, Provoco, inquit,I appeal,: si a duumviris provocarit, provocatione certato,; : ab omni judicio poenāque provocari licere,.—
Act., to appeal to a judge (post-class.): si judicem provocent,: si praefectus urbi judicem dederit, ipse erit provocandus, qui eum judicem dederit,.—Also: provocare judicium ad populum,to bring the decision before the people by appeal,; rarely, aliquem ad judicem,to cite, summon before,.—
Trop.
To challenge to a contest, to contend with, emulate, rival, vie with (post-Aug.): aliquem virtute,to vie with him in virtue,: elegia Graecos provocamus,; cf.: ea pictura naturam ipsam provocavit,.—Of things, : immensum latus Circi templorum pulchritudinem provocat,.—
To challenge, incite, provoke to any thing: felicitas temporum, quae bonam conscientiam civium tuorum ad usum indulgentiae tuae provocat, (7) fin.: omni comitate ad hilaritatem et jocum provocare,; : tacentes ad communionem sermonis,.—
To excite, stimulate, exasperate, stir up, rouse with any thing (class.; syn.: irrito, lacesso): qui non solum a me provocatus sed etiam suā sponte solet, etc.,: aliquem beneficio,: sermonibus,: minis et verbis,: bello,: injuriā, et saep.: ad iracundiam,; . —
To call forth, occasion, produce, cause: officia comitate,: mortem tot modis,, praef. 1, § 5: bellum,; .—
(Acc. to I. B. 2.) To appeal to any thing, to cite as authority or proof (late Lat.): ad litteras Pudentillae,: ad Judaeorum Codices provocare,.

la:noun:proverbium.html:
prōverbĭum, ĭi, n.
pro-verbum
.
An old saying, a saw, maxim, adage, proverb (class.; syn. adagium): ex quo illud factum est jam tritum sermone proverbium, etc.,; cf. : in proverbii consuetudinem venire,: illud in proverbium venit,: quod est Graecis hominibus in proverbio,; : quod proverbii loco dici solet,: proverbii locum obtinere,: vulgare,: acta agimus, quod vetamur veteri proverbio,: ut proverbium loquitur vetus,.—In plur.: in communibus proverbiis,: proverbia opportune aptata,. —
A byword, a subject of contemptuous reference (post-class.): et eris perditus in proverbium,; .

la:adj:provincialis.html:
prōvincĭālis, e, adj.
provincia
,
of or belonging to a province, provincial: administratio,: scientia,the administration of a province,, § 20: edictum,belonging to a province,: molestia,arising from the administration of a province,: abstinentia,observed in the administration of a province,: integritas,: ornamenta et commoda,: parsimonia,: bellum,: crimina,: aditus ad me minime provinciales,not as they usually are with provincial administrators,.—
Subst.: prōvincĭālis, is, m., an inhabitant of a province; mostly in plur., the people of a province, provincials, ; ; . —Opp. to the inhabitants of Italy: Italicus es an provincialis?; ; cf. as adj., .

la:verb:proveho.gloss: to carry or conduct forward or along
senses: to carry or conduct forward or along
to proceed, advance, move, drive, ride, sail etc. to a place
la:verb:proveho.html:
prō-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a.,
to carry or conduct forwards, to carry or convey along, to conduct, convey, transport, etc., to a place; and freq. pass. in mid. signif., to go, proceed, advance, move, drive, ride, sail, etc., to a place (freq. and class.).
Lit.: eam pol provexi: avehere non quivi,I took her on board the ship,: alvos apum mulis,: aër a tergo quasi provehat atque propellat,.—Mid.: cum classe freto provehi,; : provehimur portu,: huc se provecti deserto in litore condunt,; : provectus equo,: a terrā provectae naves,: naves provectae in altum,—
Trop., to carry on, along, or forwards, to lead on; to promote, advance, exalt, raise: ecquo te tua virtus provexisset?promoted, exalted,: ad summos honores alios scientia juris provexit,; so, quosdam infimi generis ad amplissimos honores,; and: aliquem in consulatūs, censuras et triumphos,; cf.: studiosos amat, fovet, provehit,: vim temperatam di quoque provehunt In majus,: haec spes provexit, ut ad conspecta procul pecora decurrerent, carried them so far, brought them to such a pitch, that, etc., ; cf. absol.: illo etiam (forsitan pravo) gaudio provehente, quod, etc.,: quem e gregario milite Alexander virtutis causā provexerat,: quos (reges) ad fastigium majestatis spectata moderatio provehebat,: quos provexerat, fortuna destitit,: in consulare provectus fuerat vestigium,: vitam in altum, qs. to drive it into a sea, i. e. into disquietude, .—
Mid., to advance, proceed, go onwards, make progress, etc.: ne videlicet ultra quam homini datum est nostra provehantur,: sentio me esse longius provectum quam proposita ratio postularet,have been carried farther, have gone farther,: quod si qui longius in amicitiā provecti essent,: provectus longius quam voluit, id. Har.

Resp. 20, 43: imbecillitas in altum provehitur,: provehi in maledicta,: per altercationem ad continuas et infestas orationes provecti sunt,.—

Of speech, to draw out, protract, prolong: orationem,: quid ultra Provehor?why do I say more?.—Hence, prōvectus, a, um, P. a. of time, advanced: eum colere coepi non admodum grandem natu, sed tamen jam aetate provectum,: provectā aetate mortua est,: provecta nox erat,: cum aetate jam provectus esset,: senectute provectior,; : equis provectioribus tempora cavari incipiunt,: aetatis provectae,.

la:verb:provolvo.gloss: to roll or tumble forwards, along, over and over or away
senses: to roll or tumble forwards, along, over and over or away
to cast oneself down, fall down, prostrate oneself; descend
to snatch away, carry away, hurry on
la:verb:provolvo.html:
prō-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a.
Lit.
In gen., to roll or tumble forwards, to roll along, roll over and over, roll away (class., but not in Cic.): aliquem in viam mediam,: corpora,: ubi glaeba e terrā provolvitur ingens,: cupas ardentes in opera,: congestas lapidum moles,: Galba projectus e sellā ac provolutus est,; ; .—
In partic., with se or mid., to cast one's self down, fall down, prostrate one's self at another's feet (syn. prosterno): se alicui ad pedes,: flentes ad genua consulis provolvuntur,: provolutae ad pedes,: genibus ejus provolutus,; ; .—
Trop., to snatch away, carry away, hurry on (post-Aug.): multi fortunis provolvebantur,i. e. are ruined,.—
Mid., to humble one's self: usque ad libita Pallantis provoluta,submitting to the desires of,: provolutus effususque in iram,.

la:verb:provenio.html:
prō-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. n.,
to come forth, appear (not in Cic.; syn. appareo).
Lit.
In gen. (mostly anteclass.): proveniebant oratores novi, Naev. ap. (Com. Rel. p. 14 Rib.): scriptorum magna ingenia,: in scenam,: quibus feminis menstrua non proveniunt,.—
In partic.
To come forth, be brought forth, be born; to originate, arise, be produced (post-Aug.; cf. progigno): deductis olim, quique mox provenere, haec patria est,were born,: neque Artemenem Dario provenisse,: nec aliud ibi animal provenit,; : insula, in quā candidum plumbum provenit,: lana,; : sic neque fistulosus (caseus) neque salsus neque aridus provenit,.—
To grow up, grow, thrive (so in Cæs. and Livy; cf. redeo): frumentum propter siccitates angustius provenerat,; ; ; : virgas roscidas si recideris, parum prospere proveniunt,; ; ; : arbores sponte suā provenientes,: cum provenisset segetum copia,; .—
Trop.
In gen., to come forth, appear (very rare): malum maximum, si id provenit,.—
In partic.
To spring, originate, arise; to come to pass, take place, to happen, occur (cf.: accido, evenio): carmina proveniunt animo deducta sereno,: ut ex studiis gaudium, sic studia hilaritate proveniunt,; cf.: Alexandro simile provenisset ostentum,: provenire certa ratione,.—
To go on, proceed in any manner; to succeed, prosper, flourish, turn out: decumae proveniunt male, Lucil. ap. .—Transf., of personal subjects, to whom any thing turns out in any manner: cum tu recte provenisti,since it has turned out well with you,; ; ; cf.: nequiter multis modis,; : novā ubertate provenire terram,flourish,; .—
Pregn., to go on well, to prosper, succeed, = succedere: si destinata provenissent,: si consilium provenisset,: provenere dominationes,: ut proveniant sine malo,: ut initia belli provenissent,; .

la:noun:providentia.gloss: The ability to see something in advance; foresight, foreknowledge.
senses: The ability to see something in advance; foresight, foreknowledge.
la:noun:providentia.html:
prōvĭdentĭa, ae, f.
provideo
.
Foresight, foreknowledge: providentia est, per quam futurum aliquid videtur ante quam factum sit,: timoris tormentum memoria reducit, providentia anticipat,.—
Foresight, forethought, forecast, precaution, providence (cf. prudentia): deorum providentiā mundum administrari,; cf. ; ; : alterum ex providentiā timorem afferre solet,: plurimum tibi et usus et providentiae superest,: jam te providentia deorum primum in locum provexerat,.—With object. gen.: neque feriendi neque declinandi providentia,: providentia filiorum suorum,—In plur.: agnosce bonitatem dei ex providentiis,—
Transf.
The government of the world by infinite wisdom and foresight, providence (post-class.): tua, Pater, providentia gubernat,; .—
Providence, as a designation of the Deity (post-Aug.): vis illum (deum) providentiam dicere? recte dices,: oratio, quā nihil praestantius homini dedit providentia,; ; praef. § 4; 5, 12, 19; 10, 1, 109; 12, 1, 2; .—
Providentia, Providence, personified as a goddess, a transl. of the Gr. Πρόνοια, .

prō-vĭdĕo, vīdi, vīsum, 2, v. n. and a.
Neutr.
Lit., to see forwards or before one's self, to see in the distance, to discern, descry (very rare): ubi, quid petatur, procul provideri nequeat,.—
Trop.
To be provident or cautious, to act with foresight, to take care (rare but class.; syn. praecaveo): actum de te est, nisi provides. ; : nisi providisses, tibi ipsi pereundum fuisset,.—
To see to, look after, care for; to provide, make preparation or provision for any thing (freq. and class.); constr. absol., with dat., de, ut, ne: multum in posterum providerunt, quod, etc., : nihil me curassis, ego mihi providero,: rei frumentariae,: condicioni omnium civium,: ut consulas omnibus, ut provideas saluti,.—Impers. pass.: a dis vitae hominum consuli et provideri,: est autem de Brundusio providendum,; cf.: de re frumentariā,: de frumento,: ut quam rectissime agantur omnia providebo,.—So with ne, : cura et provide, ne quid ei desit,: ne qua civitas suis finibus recipiat, a me provisum est,; cf. impers.: provisum est, ne, etc.,: provisum atque praecautum est, ne quid, etc.,.—
Act.
Lit., to see or perceive in the distance (very rare): nave provisā,; .—
Trop.
In respect of time, to see or perceive beforehand, to foresee; to see before or earlier (class.): si qui, quae eventura sunt, provideant, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 407 Rib.); cf. : rem, quam mens providit,: quod ego, priusquam loqui coepisti, sensi atque providi,; cf. : medicus morbum ingravescentem ratione providet, insidias imperator, tempestates gubernator,: providere, quid futurum sit,: quod adhuc conjecturā provideri possit,: tempestas ante provisa,: ratio explorata atque provisa,: non hercle te provideram,: aliquem,.—
To see to, look after, care for, give attention to; to prepare or provide for any thing: eas cellas provident, ne habeant in solo umorem,: ut res tempusque postulat, provideas atque administres,: providentia haec potissimum providet, ut, etc.,: omnia,: ea, quae ad usum navium pertinerent,: rem frumentariam,; cf.: frumento exercitui proviso,: provisi ante commeatūs,: verbaque provisam rem non invita sequentur,: omnia quae multo ante memoi provisa repones,; cf.: providebam Dominum in conspectu meo, kept in view, i. e. in mind, .—
Providere aliquid, to prevent, obviate an evil (syn. cavere): neque omnino facere aut providere quicquam poterant, Kritz: quicquid provideri potest, provide,: quae consilio provideri poterunt, cavebuntur,; ; Sillig; 34, 7, 18, § 40; .—Hence,
prōvĭ-dens, entis, P. a., foreseeing, provident, prudent (class.): homo multum providens,.—Comp.: id est providentius,more prudent,.—Sup.: providentissimus quisque,; .—Adv.: prōvĭdenter, with foresight, providently, prudently, ; ; .—Comp.: quanto melius quanto providentius,.—Sup.: providentissime,; (69), 1; 10, 77 (81), 1.—*
prōvīsō, adv., with foresight or forethought, prudently: temere, proviso,.

la:noun:provisio.html:
prōvīsĭo, ōnis, f.
provideo
.
A foreseeing, foreknowing: provisio animi,.—
Foresight, providence: genus longā animi provisione fugiendum,.—
Forethought, precaution for a thing: posteri temporis,: annonaria, i. e. a providing with provisions, purveying, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 18.—
Hindrance, prevention of a thing: horum incommodorum una cautio est atque una provisio, ut, etc.,.

la:verb:provolvo#2.html:
prō-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a.
Lit.
In gen., to roll or tumble forwards, to roll along, roll over and over, roll away (class., but not in Cic.): aliquem in viam mediam,: corpora,: ubi glaeba e terrā provolvitur ingens,: cupas ardentes in opera,: congestas lapidum moles,: Galba projectus e sellā ac provolutus est,; ; .—
In partic., with se or mid., to cast one's self down, fall down, prostrate one's self at another's feet (syn. prosterno): se alicui ad pedes,: flentes ad genua consulis provolvuntur,: provolutae ad pedes,: genibus ejus provolutus,; ; .—
Trop., to snatch away, carry away, hurry on (post-Aug.): multi fortunis provolvebantur,i. e. are ruined,.—
Mid., to humble one's self: usque ad libita Pallantis provoluta,submitting to the desires of,: provolutus effususque in iram,.

la:noun:proventus.html:
prōventus, ūs, m.
provenio
,
a coming forth, growing up, growth, increase; produce, yield, crop (not in Cic.; syn. reditus).
Lit.: proventu oneret sulcos,: papilionis,: rosarum,: olei,: lactis,: uberi vinearum proventu,: ficus trifero proventu,; ; ; ; cf.: equinus proventus,.— In plur.: frugum,; ; .—
Transf., a supply, number: tum deinde efflorescat... oratorum ingens proventus,: poëtarum,: clarorum virorum,: murium,: cuniculorum,.—
Trop.
In gen., an issue, result: errare, si qui in bello omnis secundos rerum proventus expectent,: omnes milites intenti pugnae proventum expectabant,: hujus peregrinationis,.—
In partic., a fortunate issue, happy result, success: superioris temporis,: secundarum rerum,: orationis,; .

la:verb:provenio#2.html:
prō-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. n.,
to come forth, appear (not in Cic.; syn. appareo).
Lit.
In gen. (mostly anteclass.): proveniebant oratores novi, Naev. ap. (Com. Rel. p. 14 Rib.): scriptorum magna ingenia,: in scenam,: quibus feminis menstrua non proveniunt,.—
In partic.
To come forth, be brought forth, be born; to originate, arise, be produced (post-Aug.; cf. progigno): deductis olim, quique mox provenere, haec patria est,were born,: neque Artemenem Dario provenisse,: nec aliud ibi animal provenit,; : insula, in quā candidum plumbum provenit,: lana,; : sic neque fistulosus (caseus) neque salsus neque aridus provenit,.—
To grow up, grow, thrive (so in Cæs. and Livy; cf. redeo): frumentum propter siccitates angustius provenerat,; ; ; : virgas roscidas si recideris, parum prospere proveniunt,; ; ; : arbores sponte suā provenientes,: cum provenisset segetum copia,; .—
Trop.
In gen., to come forth, appear (very rare): malum maximum, si id provenit,.—
In partic.
To spring, originate, arise; to come to pass, take place, to happen, occur (cf.: accido, evenio): carmina proveniunt animo deducta sereno,: ut ex studiis gaudium, sic studia hilaritate proveniunt,; cf.: Alexandro simile provenisset ostentum,: provenire certa ratione,.—
To go on, proceed in any manner; to succeed, prosper, flourish, turn out: decumae proveniunt male, Lucil. ap. .—Transf., of personal subjects, to whom any thing turns out in any manner: cum tu recte provenisti,since it has turned out well with you,; ; ; cf.: nequiter multis modis,; : novā ubertate provenire terram,flourish,; .—
Pregn., to go on well, to prosper, succeed, = succedere: si destinata provenissent,: si consilium provenisset,: provenere dominationes,: ut proveniant sine malo,: ut initia belli provenissent,; .

la:verb:provolo.html:
prō-vŏlo, āvi, 1, v. n.,
to fly forth.
Lit., : apes,.—
Transf., to hurry or hasten forth, to rush out (class.): capillo passo in viam provolarunt, Quadrig. ap. : subito omnibus copiis provolaverunt,: in primum infestis hastis provolant duo Fabii,; cf. : ad primores provolat,: formicae provolant,.— Of things: sonitus provolat ictu, flies forth or out, .

la:noun:provocatio.html:
prōvŏcātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
A calling out, summoning, challenging to combat (post-Aug.): ex provocatione hostem interemit,; ; ; .—
A stimulus, provocation, encouragement (late Lat.): in provocationem caritatis,. —
A citation before a higher tribunal, an appeal (freq. and class.): ad populum provocatio esto,; cf.: Publicola legem ad populum tulit ... ne quis magistratus civem Romanum adversus provocationem necaret neve verberaret,; ; ; 3, 32, 44; ; ; : provocationem interponere,to appeal,: est provocatio,an appeal lies,; : appellatio provocatioque, et saep.; Plin. praef. § 10.—In plur.: provocationes omnium rerum,.

id.
.
